label: Grief & losing someone
title: Bhagavad Gita on Death of a Loved One: 7 Verses for Grief
description: Seven gentle verses for after a loss: what death ends and what it doesn't, from Krishna's first teaching (2.20, 2.22, 2.23). Sanskrit, plain English and one small thing to do.
h1: Bhagavad Gita on the death of a loved one: 7 verses for grief
subtitle: For the weeks after a loss. Read slowly, one at a time, whenever you can.
keywords: bhagavad gita on death of loved ones
gita verses for someone who passed away
intro: The Gita begins with grief. Arjuna sits down in his chariot, unable to face losing the people he loves, and Krishna's first teaching (2.11 to 2.30) is about death: what ends and what does not. These verses stay with that teaching. You can keep grieving while you read them. They give the grief a wider frame: the self that was never born and does not die, worn clothes set aside, the unseen before and after. The last is Bharata in the Ramayana, coming home too late.

image.alt: A woman holding her late father's shawl beside his garlanded photograph and a lit diya
image.altGlobal: A woman holding her late father's cardigan beside his photograph and a lit candle

days.heading: What was never born doesn't die
days.line: The self was never born and never dies. It is not killed when the body is.
days.forYou: Na jāyate mriyate vā kadācit. Krishna's first comfort is about the person you love. What made them who they were, the self, was never born and does not die when the body does. Take in as much of it as you can today, and let it sit beside the grief.
days.today: Say their name out loud today, in a sentence that starts with 'I remember'.
days.note: Mourn fully. This verse is comfort about what remains.

days.heading: Worn clothes, set aside
days.line: As we drop worn-out clothes and put on new ones, the self leaves a worn body for a new one.
days.forYou: This is the Gita's best-known picture of death: as we set aside worn clothes for new ones, the self leaves a worn-out body. Krishna offers it to the one grieving. Hold it for yourself, and be careful offering it to someone else in fresh pain.
days.today: If you have something of theirs, hold it for a minute. Let yourself feel whatever comes.

days.heading: Childhood, youth, age, and on
days.line: Childhood, youth, old age: the body keeps changing. The wise stay steady through the next change too.
days.forYou: You already watched the person you love change, from a younger self to the one you last knew. Krishna asks you to see death as one more change the self passes through. He says the wise are not bewildered by it. In the first weeks, being bewildered is allowed.
days.today: Look at one old photo of them at a different age. Notice that it's still them.

days.heading: Nothing can touch it
days.line: No weapon cuts it, no fire burns it, no water wets it, no wind dries it.
days.forYou: Nainaṃ chindanti śastrāṇi. No weapon cuts the self, no fire burns it, no water wets it, no wind dries it. Whatever happened to the body at the end, through illness, accident or age, did not reach who they were.
days.today: If the last days were hard to watch, read this verse slowly, twice.

days.heading: We only see the middle
days.line: We come from the unseen and return to it; only the middle is visible.
days.forYou: Before birth we can't see one another, after death we can't, and only the middle is visible. Krishna widens the frame. Arjuna weeps through this teaching and Krishna keeps teaching him, tears and all. The verse gives the loss something larger to rest in.
days.today: Write down one thing about them that you saw in 'the middle' and want to keep.
days.note: Grief is natural, and tears are part of it. The verse widens the frame.

days.heading: A leaf, a flower, a little water
days.line: A leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water: whatever is offered with love, I accept.
days.forYou: Krishna says that whatever is offered with love, even a leaf, a flower or a little water, is accepted. Many families remember their dead with exactly these things: water, flowers, a lamp. Love needs somewhere to go, and a small offering gives it a place.
days.today: Make one small offering in their memory today: a lamp, a flower, some water, or a kindness done in their name.

days.heading: Coming home too late

story.title: Bharata returns to Ayodhya
story.body: Bharata was far away at his grandfather's home when his father, King Dasharatha, died. Messengers called him back without telling him why. He rode into an Ayodhya that had gone quiet, went looking for his father, and learned he was gone. He fell to the ground and wept. When he could stand again, the family priest Vasishtha gently told him it was time to perform the last rites, and he did them, grieving as he went.
story.lesson: Missing the goodbye is its own grief. Let yourself feel it, then do what love asks next.

days.forYou: If you weren't there at the end, because of distance, work or a hospital's rules, Bharata's grief is yours. The Ramayana lets him fall and weep, and then gives him something to do for his father.
days.today: If something is left undone for them, a call, a letter, a rite, choose one and do it this week.

verse.sanskrit: अम्ब केनात्यगाद् राजा व्याधिना मय्यनागते । धन्या रामादयः सर्वे यैः पिता संस्कृतः स्वयम् ॥
verse.line: He died while I was away. Blessed are those who were there to say goodbye.

faq.q: What does the Bhagavad Gita say about the death of a loved one?
faq.a: Krishna's first teaching (2.11 to 2.30) speaks to it directly: the self (ātman) is never born and never dies (2.20), leaves a worn body as we change clothes (2.22), and cannot be harmed by weapons, fire, water or wind (2.23). He widens the frame without denying the loss.

faq.q: Which Gita verse is read for someone who has passed away?
faq.a: 2.20 and 2.22 are the most often read, and 2.23 (nainaṃ chindanti śastrāṇi) is close behind. Many families read from chapter 2 during the days of mourning.

faq.q: Does the Gita say it is wrong to grieve?
faq.a: No. Krishna speaks to Arjuna's despair, and he never asks him to love his family less. The verses widen the frame around a loss. If grief is overwhelming you, please talk to someone you trust or a counsellor.
